To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The monocytes, macro-phages, and dend-ritic cells of the mouse are generated by a common precursor in the bone marrow; and 2) The monocytes of the mouse are derived from a distinct precursor that is distinct from the precursors of tissue macrophages and dendritic cells.

(1) monocytes and macrophage subsets are generated by the differentiation of common precursors, and that the differentiation of these cells in the steady state is controlled by a balance of signals provided by hematopoietic stem cells and by the microenvironment of the bone marrow; (2) monocyte differentiation in the steady state occurs in a stepwise fashion, with the first differentiation step leading to the generation of a subset of immature myeloid cells (monoblasts), and

(a) monocytes and dendritic cells are closely related to each other, (b) the monocyte and dendritic cell lineages are closely related to the macrophage lineage, (c) the monocyte lineage and the macrophage lineages are closely linked, and (d) monocyte and dendrite cell development is regulated by a combination of signals that includes the transcription factor PU.1 and the cytokine M-CSF

The main takeaway from our work is that

myeloid lineage cells are not a homogeneous population of cells, but rather, they are a collection of functionally distinct subsets that are defined by their anatomical locations, developmental origins, and differentiation cues.

the monocytes, tissue macrophages and dendritic cells are not as distinct as previously thought, and the developmental pathways that lead to the different cell populations are more complex and intertwined than we had previously imagined.
the development of myeloid cells is not a single pathway but rather is a complex process that is influenced by many cell-intrinsic factors and environmental cues.
